title: Days, months, dates
goal: Master the Estonian calendar — and discover that you already know most of the twelve month names.
bekal: name the seven days and twelve months
say something happens **on** a given day or in a given month
give dates and recognize Estonian holidays

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mis kuupäev täna on?

notes: **Estonian and English month names are near-twins** because both borrow from the same Latin source — Estonian through German, English through Old French and Latin. These are twelve words you barely need to learn, only adjust the spelling.

**The first four days are numbers.** *Esmaspäev* = first day, *teisipäev* = second day, *kolmapäev* = third, *neljapäev* = fourth. The other three have different origins: *reede* from German, *laupäev* from a Norse word for "bath day", *pühapäev* = "holy day".

⚠️ **Estonian numbers its weekdays; English names them after gods.** *Wednesday* is Woden's day, *Thursday* Thor's day. Estonian instead counts: **number the working days, give special names to the weekend**. Budi's Indonesian numbers its days too, via Arabic (Senin = "second").
**Kolmekümnendal aprillil** — "on the thirtieth of April". Both words take the ending **-l**: the date is an ordinal + *-l*, and the month also takes *-l*. This pattern works for all dates.

grammars.title: Seven days — four of them numbers
body: The third column is the form you actually use: "on that day", with the ending **-l**.
after: ⚠️ Estonian counts from **Monday as day one**, so *kolmapäev* is the "third day" — Wednesday. (The Arabic counting behind Indonesian starts from Sunday, which is why Budi's *Senin* is "second".)
*Nädal* means week (seven days), *nädalavahetus* means weekend (literally: "week change"). *Sel nädalal* = this week, *järgmisel nädalal* = next week, *eelmisel nädalal* = last week.
For repeated habits, the day is used in the plural + *-ti*: *esmaspäeviti* (every Monday), *reedeti* (every Friday), *hommikuti* (every morning).

grammars.title: Twelve months you already have
body: Read the second and fourth columns side by side. Almost nothing needs memorizing — only spelling adjustments.
after: ⚠️ Month names are written in **lowercase** in Estonian, like language names and nationalities. This is the opposite of English.

Notice that *september, oktoober, november, detsember* lose their final *e* when an ending is added: *septembris*, not "septemberis". The same shortening pattern as *number → numbri* and *sõber → sõbra* in unit 6.

Months take **-s** (the inside series), while days and dates take **-l** (the surface series). *Mais* (in May), but *esmaspäeval* (on Monday) and *kolmandal mail* (on the third of May). There is no logic to find; memorize the pairs.

English

blocks.title: ⚠️ Kuu has two meanings — just like "moon/month"
items: *kuu* means both the **moon in the sky** and the **calendar month**. English once did too: *month* comes from *moon*.
*Kuu on täna täis.* — The moon is full today. *Ma olen siin kolm kuud.* — I've been here three months.
English now has two separate words (*moon* and *month*), so here Estonian gives you one word to learn instead of two.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Jaanipäev is the real holiday in Estonia**, for many people bigger than Christmas. The cities genuinely empty out; everyone goes to the countryside, lights bonfires, and stays up under a sky that never gets dark. If you're in Estonia on June 23–24, don't expect shops or offices to be open.

blocks.title: Holiday greetings
items: ⚠️ Notice that they all use *head/häid* — forms of *hea* (good). Estonian offers greetings by wishing "good ones" without a verb, just like *head aega* and *head isu*.
